explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. At Beersheba he offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. New country ahead, a long road behind, and the first thing on his list is God. My list usually starts with "preheat the oven," so Jacob has better priorities than I do.

explanations.answer: He digs a new well for water
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd think that, since a long trip makes a man think about water. But the text never mentions a well here. It says he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. Isaac was Jacob's father, and Jacob worships the same God. That's a lot less shoveling than a well would have been.

explanations.answer: He buys grain for the long trip
explanations.explanation: Packing for the road is smart, but the text never says Jacob bought anything at Beersheba. It says he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. If I were packing, I'd bring a whole box of cookies and call it prepared. Jacob's stop was about worship.

Yes, baker. God says, “…I will make you into a great nation there.” Think about that for a second. It's one old man with his family on the road, and God calls him a future nation. That's a big promise from the One who makes it.
An army sounds strong, I'll give you that. But God doesn't say army. He says, “…I will make you into a great nation there.” A nation is bigger than a bunch of soldiers. It's a whole people.
A city is a nice thought, with streets and maybe a bakery on the corner. But God doesn't say city. He says, “…I will make you into a great nation there.” A nation is a whole lot bigger than one city.
That's right. God tells Jacob, “I will go down with you to Egypt…” Jacob isn't headed down there on his own. He has family around him, and he has God's word that God goes with him.
It's actually true, friend. God tells Jacob, “I will go down with you to Egypt…” That's God's own promise, spoken right to him in the vision. Jacob doesn't make that trip alone.
Yes, baker. God says, “…I will surely bring you back.” He doesn't just promise to go down there with Jacob. He promises to bring him back, and that word "surely" is a strong one.

Big thinking, but God doesn't say that. He says He will make Jacob into a great nation there, and that He will surely bring him back. Nothing in the vision hands Jacob the whole country of Egypt. Even I wouldn't hand over a whole country for one batch of cookies.

A crown would be something, wouldn't it? But God never says king. He says, “I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back.” That's the promise God makes right after He says Jacob doesn't need to be afraid.

I get the thought, since moving a big family is a lot to carry. But the text says the opposite. "They also took the livestock and possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan." That's a paraphrase, but the point is plain. The flocks and herds go down to Egypt with them.

Right, baker. The text says they took the livestock and the possessions they had acquired in Canaan, and Jacob and all his offspring went to Egypt. Nobody left the flocks at home. That's a lot of moving for one trip.

That's him, baker. Judah, one of Jacob's sons, is the one Jacob sends ahead to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. Jacob picks one son to go first and find the way. I wouldn't send me, because I get lost between the oven and the counter.

Close, since Reuben is the first one named in the list, Jacob's firstborn. But the text says Jacob sent Judah ahead to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. Judah, another of Jacob's sons, makes the trip first.
It makes sense you'd think of him, since Benjamin is Joseph's brother, a son of Rachel. But the text says Jacob sent Judah ahead to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. Benjamin isn't the one sent.

Joseph is a big man in Egypt, so I see why you'd picture him staying put. But the text says Joseph presented himself to his father, embraced him, and wept profusely. That's no greeting from a distance. He holds his father.
Yes, baker. Joseph presented himself to his father, embraced him, and wept profusely. There's no wave from the chariot and no formal nod. It's a long hug with a whole lot of tears.

explanations.answer: He has seen Joseph is still alive
explanations.explanation: That's it. Israel says, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!” He's looking right at the son he'd been told was gone. I think this is a man who finally gets to put the heavy thing down.

explanations.answer: He is too worn out to go on
explanations.explanation: The trip was long, so I get it. But the text never says Israel is worn out. He says, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!” His words are about seeing Joseph's face.

explanations.answer: He knows Canaan is lost for good
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything like that. Israel says, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!” It's about Joseph, not about the land. And God had already told him, “I will surely bring you back” (Genesis 46:4).

You got it, baker. Joseph tells them to say they have raised livestock since they were young, and that their fathers did too. It's a true answer, because shepherds are exactly what they are. Joseph's coaching them to say what's real.

It's actually true, friend. Joseph tells his brothers to say their servants have raised livestock ever since their youth, both they and their fathers. That's the exact answer he gives them for Pharaoh's question. It's also just who they are.

Yes, baker. Joseph says they'll be allowed to settle in Goshen, “…since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.” So the brothers say they're shepherds, plain and honest. The very thing the Egyptians dislike gets them a place of their own.

That would be a sweet deal, but taxes never come up. Joseph's reason is that all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians. That's why telling Pharaoh they raise livestock gets them settled in Goshen.

That's a fair guess, but the text doesn't say it. Joseph's reason is, “…all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.” Nothing is said about whether the land is claimed or not. The reason Joseph gives is about the Egyptians and shepherds.

explanations.answer: There's no pasture for their flocks
explanations.explanation: That's right. They tell Pharaoh, “…there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants, since the famine in the land of Canaan has been severe.” Shepherds need grass for their flocks, and back home there isn't any. It's a plain answer for a hard time.

explanations.answer: Their wells in Canaan have run dry
explanations.explanation: Water is a worry for flocks, I know. But the brothers never mention wells. They say there is no pasture for the flocks, since the famine in Canaan has been severe.

That makes for a dramatic story, but it isn't what they say. They tell Pharaoh there is no pasture for their flocks because the famine in Canaan has been severe. No enemies are mentioned. It's a famine and hungry flocks.

I can see why you'd think so, since the brothers did come asking for a favor. But Pharaoh says the opposite. He tells Joseph, “…settle your father and brothers in the best part of the land.” That's a generous welcome.
Right, baker. Pharaoh says, “…settle your father and brothers in the best part of the land.” They get the best, not the leftovers. The king is generous here.
Yes, baker. Pharaoh says, “…put them in charge of my own livestock.” These brothers have raised flocks since they were young. Pharaoh has animals that need that kind of experience.
That's a thought, since Joseph is the one who handles Egypt's food. But Pharaoh's offer is, “…put them in charge of my own livestock.” The talented men are shepherds, so livestock fits.
Chariots are flashy, I'll admit. But Pharaoh says, “…put them in charge of my own livestock.” That's the work these brothers have known all their lives.

That's right. Joseph brings in his father Jacob and presents him before Pharaoh, Egypt's king, and Jacob blesses him. An old shepherd from Canaan stands in front of the most powerful man around, and he gives a blessing instead of asking for one.
It's actually true, friend. Joseph presents his father before Pharaoh, Egypt's king, and Jacob blesses him. The text says it right there. He's the one doing the blessing.
That's the number, baker. Jacob says, “My travels have lasted 130 years…” Notice he calls them his travels. That's how he describes a long life on the road.
Not quite, but you're in the neighborhood. Jacob says, “My travels have lasted 130 years…” That's ten more than your pick. It's a lot of road.

That's a big number, and it's a real one from the family. Abraham, Jacob's grandfather, lived a hundred and seventy-five years (Genesis 25:7). But Jacob says, “My travels have lasted 130 years…” Jacob's own number is lower.
Yes, baker. Jacob says, “My years have been few and hard…” That's an honest answer, and I think a tender one. He doesn't dress it up for the king.
That's the opposite of what Jacob says. He tells Pharaoh, “My years have been few and hard, and they have not matched the years of the travels of my fathers.” Few, not long, and hard, not easy.

It would be nice if his years were quiet, but that isn't what he says. Jacob tells Pharaoh, “My years have been few and hard…” He compares them to the years of his fathers' travels, and says they haven't matched.

That's right, baker. The text says Joseph provided his father and brothers and all his father's household with food for their families. Land is nice, but a family has to eat. Joseph makes sure that gets done.

That would be fancy, but the text doesn't say it. After the property, it says Joseph provided his father's household with food for their families. Pharaoh's offer was about the best of the land and a job over his livestock.

That sounds comfortable, but servants aren't mentioned. The text says Joseph provided his father and brothers and all his father's household with food for their families. It's a quiet, practical kind of care.
